890.title: The universe in his mouth
890.hook: Yashoda looks in her toddler's mouth for dirt and sees the whole universe, herself included
890.carry: the little one holds the whole universe
890.howItsDone: Krishna devotees tell this story alongside the butter-thief stories, and devotional paintings and songs show Yashoda peering into the child's open mouth.

segments.voice: Last week ended with the butter thief dragging a mortar between two trees, and two cursed brothers walking free. Your line was darshan: to see the Lord, and be seen.

Mother, Krishna ate dirt! The other boys come running to tell on him, his older brother Balarama among them. He has just put a handful of earth in his mouth. Yashoda grabs him by the hand, scolds him, and asks why. And the little boy, dirt on his lips, looks his mother in the eye and denies everything.

I didn't eat any dirt, Mother. They're lying. If you think they're telling the truth, look in my mouth yourself. So he opens it, and she looks in. And there, inside her son's mouth, she sees everything. The Bhagavata lists it all: the sky and the directions, the mountains, the islands and oceans, the whole round earth, wind and fire, the moon and the stars. The turning of time. The gods. The elements that make up a body, and the mind itself. And in among all of it, the village of Vraja, and in the village, herself. She's standing in her yard looking into her son's mouth, and inside it she finds her yard, and herself standing in it. She's frightened. Is this a dream? Is this an illusion sent by God? Is my own mind confused? Or is it some power that belongs to my child? So she bows, inwardly, to the one beyond all thought, in whom all of this rests. Here's the teaching, and it's one of Hinduism's biggest. The God Hindus love as a little boy is not a small god. The baby she nurses, the one who steals the neighbors' butter, holds everything that is, her included. Teachers often set this beside the Bhagavad Gita, where Arjuna sees the whole universe inside Krishna on a battlefield, and trembles. Yashoda sees it in her own yard. That's why a Hindu family can keep a tiny brass baby Krishna on the shrine, feed him and rock him, and still pray to him as Lord of everything. The small form doesn't make God small. It makes God close enough to hold.

891.hook: Yashoda forgets the vision and goes back to simply loving her son

segments.voice: Yesterday Yashoda looked for dirt in her son's mouth and saw everything, her own village and herself inside it. Your line was the little one holds the whole universe.

It wasn't the first time. A chapter earlier, the Bhagavata tells a smaller version. Yashoda is nursing her baby, and he yawns, the way babies do. In that yawn, for an instant, she sees the sky, the earth, the stars, the oceans, mountains and forests. She trembles and shuts her eyes. Then the moment passes, and he's just a yawning baby again. So what happens to the next ordinary morning, after you've seen something like that?
screen: `A YAWN WHILE NURSING.` → `SKY, EARTH, STARS, FOR AN INSTANT.` → `WHAT HAPPENS NEXT?`

segments.voice: Back in the yard, Yashoda is still standing over her son, bewildered, bowing inwardly to whatever this is. Then the text says something startling. Krishna spreads his maya over her, his power to veil, and it takes the form of a mother's love for her son. She forgets. The vision is gone. She sets him on her lap, her heart full of affection for him, just as before. The story could have made her a great sage, seeing God in her child every moment. Instead the vision is taken back on purpose, and love replaces it. King Parikshit, listening, asks the sage telling the story: what did Nanda and Yashoda ever do, to be given a love like this? The sage answers with a former life, in which they asked for one thing: supreme devotion to the Lord, once they were born on earth. In this telling, being his parents is how that wish is granted. So the forgetting isn't a loss. It's the gift working. Hindus have a name for this way of loving God: vatsalya, a parent's love. Devotional schools such as the Gaudiya and the Pushti Marg count it among the great ways to love God: not bowing to the infinite from far away, but feeding him, scolding him, holding him. That's why, in many Hindu homes, someone wakes a small image of baby Krishna in the morning, bathes him, dresses him, offers him food before anyone else eats, and puts him to bed at night. They know what he is. Like Yashoda, they're allowed to love who he is to them.

Then eat it slowly. If you don't pray, offer that bite in thanks for someone who feeds you.

892.hook: a poisoned pool, a boy wrapped in a serpent's coils, a weeping village, and one brother smiling

segments.voice: Yesterday, maya: Yashoda saw everything, then was given back her ordinary love. Your line was vatsalya: loving God as your own child.

A hot day by the Yamuna. The boy Krishna is old enough now to take the calves and cows out to graze with his friends. Balarama isn't with them today. Desperate with thirst, the boys and the cattle drink from the river, and drop where they stand, lifeless at the water's edge. Krishna looks at them, the text says, with a glance full of nectar, and they get up, puzzled, as if waking from sleep. Something is wrong with that water.
screen: `A HOT DAY BY THE YAMUNA.` → `THEY DRINK, AND FALL.` → `A GLANCE BRINGS THEM BACK.`

segments.voice: What's wrong is Kaliya. In a deep pool of the Yamuna lives a great serpent, a naga with many hoods, whose poison has made the pool boil. Birds flying over it, the Bhagavata says, fall out of the sky. Krishna decides the river has to be clean again. He climbs a tall kadamba tree on the bank, tightens his clothes, slaps his arms like a wrestler, and jumps into the poisoned pool. Kaliya rises, furious, sees a small, dark, beautiful boy playing in his water, bites him, and wraps him in his coils. And Krishna goes still. The whole village runs to the river, even the cows, and sees him, motionless, wrapped in a serpent. The mothers weep around Yashoda. Nanda and the men start toward the water to go in after him. One person on that bank is calm. Balarama, the text says, smiles and says nothing, because he knows his brother's power. Then he holds them back. Why smile? Because he knows who is in the water. Hindus have a word for everything Krishna does in Vraja: lila, divine play. As devotees read it, a Lord who can't be harmed lets himself look caught, and the people who love him show how much they love him. The village's fear isn't silly; their love is the point. But the one they're grieving is not lost. That's why devotees still act these stories out as Krishna lila, plays where everyone on the bank already knows the ending, and still gasps. And many devotees carry this into their own hard nights: the worry is real, like Yashoda's, and so is Balarama's trust that Krishna holds the ending.

893.title: The dance on the serpent's hoods

segments.voice: Yesterday the boy went still in Kaliya's coils, the village wept on the bank, and Balarama smiled. Your line was lila: what looks like danger is his play.

Why does he go still? In the Bhagavata's telling, he isn't overpowered. It turns to the bank: his mother, his friends, the cows, all stricken. Krishna sees what his stillness is doing to the people who love him. He has stayed bound, playing the part of a mortal, the text says, only for a short time. Now he decides that's enough.
screen: `WHY DOES HE GO STILL?` → `HE SEES THE GRIEF ON THE BANK.` → `THAT'S ENOUGH.`

segments.voice: Krishna makes his body grow. The coils, holding a small boy, are suddenly stretched around something they can't contain, and Kaliya has to let go. The serpent rears up, hissing, eyes burning, breath smoking with poison, and the two circle in the water, Krishna moving around him the way Garuda, the great eagle, circles a snake, until Kaliya is worn out. Then Krishna does something stranger. He presses down the raised hoods, climbs onto them, and begins to dance. Celestial musicians gather, and drums, songs and flowers come down from the sky. Whichever hood Kaliya lifts, Krishna's feet come down on it, keeping time. Kaliya thrashes, then weakens. Blood comes from his mouths. His hoods are broken, his pride with them. And at last, exhausted, the serpent turns his mind toward the one dancing on him and, the text says, remembers the ancient Lord. What Krishna leaves undone matters. He doesn't kill Kaliya. The fight becomes a dance, and the dance goes on until the pride is gone and the serpent remembers God. Many teachers read Kaliya as the ego, ahankara in Sanskrit, the sense of me first that rears a new head every time you press one down, and its poison as what it puts into a life. In that reading, Krishna doesn't destroy the one who carries the ego. He dances it down, and what's left turns toward him. Hindus know the scene as Kaliya-mardana: a small boy, one foot raised, on a cobra's hood.

With each breath out, let it come down a little, the way Kaliya's hoods came down. If you pray, offer it to God. If you don't, simply rest there a moment, low and quiet.
Kaliya. The serpent whose coils can't hold the growing boy, and whose pride is danced out of him on his own hoods.

894.title: Spared by the feet that humbled him
894.hook: the serpent's wives plead for his life, and the marks of Krishna's feet become his protection

segments.voice: Yesterday the boy danced on Kaliya's hoods until the serpent's pride was gone, and Kaliya remembered the Lord. Your line was he humbles the ego and spares the soul.

The serpent is beaten. He lies broken in the water, the boy still standing on his heads. And out of the pool come the serpent's wives. The Bhagavata calls them the naga wives, and they don't come to fight. They come with their children in front of them, hair loose, clothes disordered, and bow before Krishna with their palms joined. Kaliya can't speak for himself anymore. So they speak for him.
screen: `THE SERPENT IS BEATEN.` → `HIS WIVES COME OUT OF THE POOL.` → `THEY SPEAK FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: What they say is surprising. They don't argue that their husband is innocent. They call his punishment fair, more than fair: a grace. Your feet have touched his head, they say, and others perform long austerities hoping for the dust of those feet. Then they ask one thing: spare him. He is our husband. Let him live. And Krishna lets him go. Kaliya, getting his breath back, speaks plainly. We serpents are born this way, angry by nature, with poison in us. It's hard to let go of what you're made of. Krishna gives him a way forward: leave this pool, go to the ocean with your family, so the river can be clean again for the people and the cows. Then Krishna names the fear that brought Kaliya here. He was hiding. Garuda, the eagle who preys on serpents, could not enter this pool because of a sage's old curse, so this poisoned corner of the Yamuna was the one place he felt safe. And Krishna answers that fear. Garuda won't harm you now, he says, because you carry the marks of my feet on your hoods. So the story ends with no one destroyed. The poison leaves the river, and the feet that broke his pride become his shelter. That's why Hindu devotion speaks so often of the Lord's lotus feet. People bow at the feet of the image in the temple. Many temples give charanamrit, water that has bathed the deity's feet, as a blessing. To take refuge at his feet, as devotees say, means this: what humbles you is also what keeps you safe.

895.title: Why the village fed a hill
895.hook: a boy asks his father why they're cooking for Indra, and the whole village turns its offering to the hill
895.carry: God is in the hill that feeds you
895.howItsDone: Some Hindu communities keep Govardhan Puja, in the days of Diwali, by building a small hill of food, called Annakut, and offering it, and pilgrims walk around Govardhan hill near Vrindavan.

segments.voice: Yesterday Kaliya was spared, sent to the ocean, and protected by the footprints on his hoods. Your line was his lotus feet humble, then protect.

The whole village is cooking. Rice, sweets, milk dishes. The elders are busy getting ready for a sacrifice. Krishna, a boy now, already knows the answer, the text says, but he goes to his father anyway and asks. Father, what's all this for? Who is it for? What do we get from it? Nanda is patient with him. It's for Indra, he says, the king of the gods, the lord of the rain clouds.
screen: `THE WHOLE VILLAGE IS COOKING.` → `"FATHER, WHAT'S THIS FOR?"` → `"FOR INDRA, LORD OF RAIN."`

segments.voice: Indra sends the rain, Nanda explains. The rain grows the grass, the grass feeds the cows, and the cows feed us. So we honor him. Krishna answers with a different picture. Beings are born and die by their own actions, he says. And what do we cowherds live by? Forests and hills. Our wealth is the cows. So let's offer to what is right in front of us: the cows, the brahmins, and the hill, Govardhan, which shelters us and our herds. Cook everything you were going to cook. Feed everyone, even the dogs, even the people at the edges of the village. Decorate the cattle, and walk around the hill. Nanda and the elders agree. Then comes a strange and lovely detail. As the people offer their food, Krishna takes on a vast new form, declares, I am the hill, and that great form eats the offerings, while the boy Krishna stands among the cowherds, bowing to it with them. That's the first Govardhan Puja. In the days around Diwali, many Hindu families and temples still keep it. They heap up an Annakut, a mountain of food, offer it to Krishna as the hill, and share it with everyone who comes. Pilgrims walk all the way around the real Govardhan, near Vrindavan, a walk of many miles. The teaching: God isn't only far off, sending rain. He's in the hill, the cows, the people you feed. Somewhere up in the sky, Indra has noticed what's missing.
screen: `INDRA SENDS RAIN; WE HONOR HIM.` · `WE LIVE BY FORESTS, HILLS, AND COWS.` · `"I AM THE HILL."` · then, large: `GOVARDHAN PUJA: A MOUNTAIN OF FOOD.`

segments.voice: At the end of a puja, many Hindus turn slowly in place, clockwise, a small circling like the cowherds walking around their hill. Stand, if you can, and turn once, slowly. With each quarter turn, name something near that holds your life up: the ground under you, the water in your tap, the people who grew your food, the people who cook it. If you pray, give thanks to God in each of them. If you don't, let gratitude rest on each one.
Govardhan lifted. It starts here: a boy asks why, and the village turns its offering toward the hill that shelters it.
Your line: God is in the hill that feeds you. Tomorrow, Indra answers with a storm. See you tomorrow.

896.title: The hill becomes a roof
896.hook: Indra sends a storm to drown the village, and Krishna lifts the hill and calls everyone under it
896.carry: sharanagati: he shelters everyone who runs to him
896.howItsDone: Krishna as Giridhari, the one who holds up the hill, is a familiar name and image in Hindu devotion, and on Govardhan Puja some communities build a small hill of food and offer it in memory of this story.

segments.voice: Yesterday a boy asked why, and the village turned its offering from Indra to the hill, the cows and the brahmins. Your line was God is in the hill that feeds you.

Indra is furious. The king of the gods has been passed over by a village of cowherds, on the advice of a child. So he calls up the clouds kept, the text says, for the end of the world, and sends them over Vraja. The sky goes black. Rain comes down in torrents, with hail, lightning and a wind that knocks over everything standing. The cows shiver and shield their calves with their bodies. The cowherds, soaked and terrified, gather around the boy who started all this. Krishna, protect us.
screen: `INDRA IS FURIOUS.` → `THE CLOUDS OF THE WORLD'S END.` → `"KRISHNA, PROTECT US."`

segments.voice: Krishna looks at the storm and understands it. This is Indra's pride, he thinks, and the people who depend on me are in danger because of it. So he walks to the hill, Govardhan, and lifts it. With one hand. The Bhagavata's picture is wonderfully small: he holds it up as easily as a child holds up a mushroom. Come under, he calls. Bring your cows, your carts, your families. Don't be afraid it will fall. And the whole village comes in under the hill, out of the rain. He holds it up for seven days, the text says, without moving, not hungry, not thirsty. Outside, Indra pours down everything he has. Under the hill, nothing reaches them. At last Indra, astonished, lets his pride give way and calls the clouds back. Krishna sets the hill back exactly where it was. This is why one of Krishna's best-loved names is Giridhari, the one who holds up the hill; the poet-saint Mirabai sang to him by that name. The teaching under it is refuge, sharanagati. The village did nothing clever. They ran to him, and he made room for every one of them, cows and carts included. Look back at the week: a mother given the grace to love him, a serpent sheltered by his feet, a village that fed the hill, and now the hill held over them all.
screen: `INDRA'S PRIDE.` · `LIFTED LIKE A MUSHROOM.` · `"COME UNDER, ALL OF YOU."` · then, large: `GIRIDHARI: REFUGE FOR ALL WHO COME.`

segments.voice: In the Pushti Marg tradition, devotees repeat a short prayer of refuge: Shri Krishna sharanam mama, Krishna is my refuge. Breathe in. Breathing out, say it softly, or in English: Krishna, you are my refuge. Let a storm in your life come to mind, and picture yourself coming in under the hill. Then think of someone who might need to come in under your roof this week. If you don't pray, remember a time something sheltered you, breathe in that dry, safe air, and hold that person there with you.
Govardhan lifted. A boy raises the hill on one hand, and a whole village and its cows shelter beneath it while the storm rages.
Your line: sharanagati: he shelters everyone who runs to him. Tomorrow, a flute in the trees. Day eight hundred ninety-six: a week, done.
